Read the frozen project document below. Write a concise technical assessment for an engineer who has not seen the project. Explain the central resource constraint, how the runtime divides resident and streamed data, why prefill and decode behave differently, and which limitations matter when interpreting benchmark numbers. End with three practical rules for evaluating future changes. Do not copy headings or sentences from the source, and keep the answer under 500 words.


--- BEGIN DOCUMENT ---
# Ember: a streamed-weights runtime for phones

Internal design memo, revision 4. Frozen for review; numbers are from the
reference phone unless a table says otherwise.

## 1. The constraint everything else follows from

A phone has one budget that matters for a language model: the amount of
memory the operating system will let a single foreground process keep
mapped before it starts terminating processes. On the reference device that
budget is about 2.1 GB for a 6 GB phone and about 3.4 GB for a 12 GB phone,
and it is enforced without warning — the process is killed, not paged. The
weights of the model we want to run occupy 4.9 GB after 4-bit quantization,
plus a projector of 380 MB when images are enabled. No arrangement of the
tensors fits the budget outright, so the runtime cannot be a loader; it has
to be a scheduler that decides, layer by layer, what is resident and what is
brought in on demand.

Two secondary constraints shape that scheduler. Flash reads on the device
sustain roughly 1.4 GB/s sequentially but fall to 180 MB/s when requests are
random and smaller than 256 KB, so the layout on disk has to be read in
long, aligned runs. And the memory bus is shared with the GPU: every byte
streamed into memory competes with the bytes the kernels are reading for
compute, so streaming faster than the model can consume buys nothing.

## 2. Resident and streamed data

Ember splits a model into two tiers and never blurs them.

**Resident data** is loaded once at model open and stays mapped for the
life of the session:

| Component | Size on the reference model | Why it is resident |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| Token embeddings | 262 MB | Read for every token on every step |
| Attention projections (all layers) | 618 MB | Small per layer, read every step, latency-critical |
| Layer norms, biases, router weights | 41 MB | Negligible size, read every step |
| KV cache (grows with context) | 0–512 MB | Written every step; cannot live on flash |
| Output head | 262 MB | Read on every decode step |

**Streamed data** is the feed-forward blocks — 3.7 GB, three quarters of the
model — which are read from the container file into a ring of eight buffer
slots of 96 MB each. A layer's feed-forward weights are decompressed into a
slot immediately before that layer executes and the slot is recycled as soon
as the layer's kernels have finished with it. The ring is sized so that the
read for layer N+2 is in flight while layer N computes; on the reference
phone the ring is 768 MB, which with the resident tier and the working set
totals about 1.9 GB, under the 6 GB phone's budget with 200 MB of headroom.

The container format stores the streamed tier in layer order, each layer's
block padded to a 4 MB boundary, with a 64-byte header per block carrying
the quantization scale layout and a checksum. The point of the padding is
the sequential-read cliff in section 1: one layer is one aligned read, and
the reader never issues a request below 4 MB. Resident tensors are stored
in a separate region at the front of the file so that model open is a
single 1.2 GB sequential read followed by a memory map, not a scatter of
small reads.

Nothing in the streamed tier is cached across steps. This is a deliberate
choice and the one most often questioned in review: an LRU cache over
feed-forward blocks would help only if the same blocks were hot across
steps, and in a dense transformer every layer runs on every token, so the
access pattern is a strict cycle and a cache smaller than the whole tier
has a hit rate of zero. The ring is the cache; its job is to hide latency,
not to reduce traffic.

## 3. Why prefill and decode behave differently

A turn has two phases with opposite bottlenecks, and the streaming design
makes the difference sharper than it is on a machine where the whole model
is resident.

**Prefill** processes the entire prompt at once. Every layer's weights are
read once from the ring and applied to hundreds or thousands of tokens, so
the work per streamed byte is high and the phase is bound by compute — on
the reference phone, by the GPU's matrix throughput. Streaming is almost
free here: a 96 MB layer read takes about 70 ms at sequential speed and the
layer's kernels take 90–140 ms for a 1,000-token prompt, so the read for the
next layer completes before the current layer finishes. Prefill throughput
on the reference phone is 210 tokens per second for a 1,000-token prompt and
falls to 160 tokens per second at 4,000 tokens as the attention cost grows.

**Decode** produces one token per step. Every layer's weights are still
read once per step, but now they are applied to a single token, so the
work per streamed byte is tiny and the phase is bound by bandwidth — first
by flash, then, once the ring is warm, by the memory bus. A decode step
must move the whole 3.7 GB streamed tier through the ring, which at 1.4
GB/s is 2.6 seconds; that is the floor, and no kernel optimization moves
it. The reference phone decodes at 0.37 tokens per second with the ring
alone.

Because that floor is unacceptable for chat, decode runs a second mechanism
that prefill does not use: **speculative reuse**. The runtime keeps the
last-decoded token's feed-forward activations and, for each layer, predicts
from the router weights (resident) which 12 percent of the feed-forward
rows will dominate the next token's output. Only those rows are streamed
for the next step; the rest are treated as zero. When the prediction is
wrong for a layer — detected by a residual-norm check against a threshold
calibrated per layer — that layer is recomputed with its full block on the
following step. On the reference phone this raises decode to 6.8 tokens per
second at a measured 3.1 percent recompute rate, with an output that matches
full-block decode on 97.4 percent of tokens in the evaluation set. The
mismatch rate is the price, and it is the number that must be reported next
to every decode figure.

Prefill does not use speculative reuse because it has nothing to
speculate from: there is no previous step for the same position, and the
compute-bound phase would not benefit from reading fewer bytes anyway. That
is why the two phases are engineered as two different programs sharing a
container, and why a change that speeds up one routinely has no effect, or
the opposite effect, on the other.

## 4. Thermal behavior

Sustained decode holds the GPU and the flash controller busy together, and
the reference phone throttles after roughly 90 seconds of continuous
generation. Measured decode falls from 6.8 to 4.9 tokens per second between
the first and fourth minute of a long answer, then stabilizes. Prefill is
affected less because it is shorter; a 4,000-token prompt finishes before
throttling begins. Any benchmark shorter than two minutes measures the
pre-throttle regime only.

## 5. Limitations that matter when reading the numbers

1. **Every figure depends on the phone's free memory at the moment of the
   run.** The ring is sized at model open from the reported budget; a phone
   with a large browser session in the background gets a smaller ring, a
   shallower prefetch, and lower decode throughput. Numbers from different
   runs are comparable only if the ring size is logged with them, and the
   harness logs it as `ring_slots` and `ring_bytes` on every line.

2. **Decode throughput is not one number.** With speculative reuse on, it
   is a pair: tokens per second and the mismatch rate against full-block
   decode. Reporting the first without the second describes a different
   model than the one that actually ran. The harness refuses to emit a
   decode line without both fields.

3. **Prefill and decode do not add.** A quoted "time to first token" is
   prefill time plus one decode step plus the container's open cost on a
   cold session; the open cost is 0.9 seconds warm and 3.4 seconds cold,
   and which one applied is recorded as `open_ms` and `open_cold`.

4. **The flash bandwidth assumption is per device, not per model.** Phones
   with slower storage move the decode floor proportionally; the same
   container on a device with 700 MB/s sequential reads decodes at
   roughly half the rate, and no amount of compute makes up the
   difference. Storage class belongs in the benchmark header.

5. **Thermal state is a hidden variable.** A run started on a warm phone
   reports the throttled regime from its first token. The harness records
   the thermal state the operating system reports at start and at end, and
   a comparison across runs with different start states is invalid.

6. **Quality numbers are from the evaluation set only.** The 97.4 percent
   token agreement was measured on prompts drawn from the same distribution
   the router thresholds were calibrated on. Out-of-distribution prompts —
   code, non-Latin scripts, long numeric tables — have shown recompute
   rates up to 11 percent and correspondingly lower decode throughput, and
   the agreement figure for them has not been measured.

7. **Image turns bypass streaming.** The projector is loaded resident for
   the duration of an image turn and evicted afterwards; its 380 MB comes
   out of the ring, which shrinks to four slots for that turn. Image-turn
   throughput therefore has its own baseline and must not be compared with
   text-turn figures.

## 6. What the harness records

Each run emits one header line and one line per phase. The header carries
the device class, storage class, reported memory budget, ring geometry,
thermal state, container revision, and quantization. The prefill line
carries prompt tokens, wall time, and tokens per second. The decode line
carries generated tokens, wall time, tokens per second, recompute rate,
mismatch rate against the reference, and the thermal state at the end.
A run whose header does not match the reference device is labeled as such
in every summary that includes it.

## 7. Open questions

- Whether the speculative-reuse threshold should adapt during a session
  from the observed recompute rate rather than stay fixed per layer.
- Whether a two-slot pinned region for the two most recompute-prone layers
  would reduce the tail latency of a wrong prediction more cheaply than
  raising the ring size.
- Whether the container should carry a second, coarser quantization of the
  streamed tier for phones below the 6 GB class, at the cost of a 1.6 GB
  larger download.

None of these change the constraint in section 1. They change how far the
runtime can get inside it.

--- END DOCUMENT ---
